content.thinking: Reviewing the labels and issues schemas to understand how labelIds are stored.

Labels are stored in a join table called `issue_labels`, not as a JSON column on issues.

The `labelIds` field comes from the join table. The migration will find all issues with the source label, add the target label where missing, remove the source label, delete it, and return the target label plus the issue count. It will reject same-source-and-target swaps and missing labels.

The migration will enforce tenant scope and project:archive permissions. It checks that both labels exist in the actor's organization. If the source and target are identical, it rejects with any error and changes nothing.

The migration will reject same-ID swaps before any database writes. It will also verify both labels exist to return a NotFoundError for missing ones.

The service must validate label equality itself, since the input may bypass Zod schema validation. The same-ID check can run before or after the permission check; neither changes data.

The same-ID check will run before any database lookup. A clear error like "Cannot merge a label into itself" will be thrown immediately to prevent any writes. Whether to still verify label existence afterward is being weighed, since tests might expect NotFoundError when the same ID is missing.

The order of checks is now settled. Existence will be verified before the same-ID check. This ensures a missing label returns NotFoundError rather than an arbitrary error. Both labels must exist in the actor's organization.

I am examining how find functions return null versus throwing errors, and reviewing typical repository find patterns.

Checking for a findLabel function. Reviewing Drizzle transaction API patterns for better-sqlite3. The relabeling merge logic belongs in the label repository, while the service layer handles permissions, not-found errors, and same-ID checks. Missing rows must trigger the existing not-found error without modifying any organization.

The service must look up both labels and throw NotFoundError before any mutation. Identical source and target labels are rejected at the service level, even when mergeLabels is called directly with unvalidated input. A successful merge replaces the source label with the target on every issue, including archived ones; issues that already carried both ends end up with only the target label.

The source label is deleted after the merge. The target label remains otherwise unchanged. The repository should return the target label and a count of issues relabelled. The service will verify both labels exist before merging.

Separate find and merge calls are safe because SQLite is a single writer and tests run sequentially. The repository will first look up both labels, then perform the mutation. The SQL will count distinct issues carrying the source label to compute the relabelled count.

The merge SQL inserts the target label for issues that carry only the source, then deletes the source rows from issue_labels and removes the source label itself. The unique index on (issue_id, label_id) must be handled carefully to avoid constraint violations.

The NOT IN clause prevents duplicate insertions when an issue already carries the target label. The join table ignores archived status, so all issues are included automatically. Every query is scoped to the actor's organization, ensuring labels from other organizations remain untouched.

The repository should also reject same-ID merges directly. A direct call without the service guard would delete all join rows and the source label, destroying data.

The same-ID guard will live in the service layer. A plain Error is sufficient since the user only requires any error to be thrown. Tests will simply verify that the call throws.

Reviewing Drizzle ORM patterns for notInArray and SQL insert-select queries.

Considering count() usage. The merge will run inside a transaction to prevent partial state on failure. better-sqlite3 Drizzle supports synchronous transactions via getDb(). Service checks will validate labels before mutating. If source and target are identical, the operation will throw before repository merge.

NotFoundError will use "Label" as the entity name. The source label is checked first; if missing, its ID appears in the error message.

Tenant scope and permission checks will follow the deleteLabel pattern: assertOrgScope first, then project:archive. Still deciding whether to validate same-ID before or after permission checks.

The spec lists tenant scope first, then permission, then existence, then same label. I will follow that order. The existence check finds the label once, so a same-ID case is rejected cleanly without extra lookups.

The same-ID guard will run in the service before any database access to prevent accidental deletion. The repository will also enforce it as a secondary safeguard. Tests only require a throw, so any error is acceptable.

Permission and tenant scope checks will run before the same-ID guard. This ensures actors without permission or from the wrong organization receive a permission-denied or tenant error instead of a same-label rejection.

Mapping out edge cases for the merge operation. If either label is missing, the mutation returns NotFound and leaves both labels untouched. When both exist, the source label is removed from issues and the target label is added instead. Issues that previously had only the source or both labels are counted in the relabelled count; issues with only the target remain unchanged. Archived issues are still relabeled, but issues in other organizations are left untouched.

Queries filter by orgId, so a label from another organization is treated as missing. The target label must remain completely unchanged after the merge, including its updatedAt timestamp. Re-reading the target from the database after the transaction completes is safer than returning the pre-merge object.

The preloaded target label will be returned directly to avoid an extra database query. The repository count will supply the issuesRelabelled value.

The repository will expose `findLabelById` and `mergeLabelInto`, returning the relabelled issue count. The service layer stays thin; the SQL merge logic lives in the repository.

Repository lookups return null, and the service layer converts that into a NotFoundError via requireFound. The merge will run inside a single transaction to prevent partial state. I am now drafting the Drizzle insert-select query using better-sqlite3.

The repository query fetches all issues linked to the source label within the organization. It then checks which of those issues already carry the target label, using an inArray filter. Only the issues missing the target label will be inserted as new rows.

The repository will insert new target-label rows, then delete the source label's join rows and the source label itself. An empty source result requires special handling to avoid invalid SQL from an inArray with no values. The same-ID guard is essential because otherwise the merge would delete all issues linked to that label.

The repository function will be named `relabelAndDeleteSource`. It throws a descriptive error when the source and target IDs are identical. The Drizzle transaction callback is synchronous for better-sqlite3, so the function can return the relabelled count directly from inside the transaction.

IssueLabel omits timestamps. "Target unchanged" means name, color, description, id, and orgId are unaffected.

SQLite limits variables to 999. A SQL insert-select avoids this for bulk label updates. The target label ID may not map correctly in the Drizzle ORM query.

Drizzle's insert-select API is being weighed against raw SQL for the bulk label update. The better-sqlite3 driver requires synchronous `.run()` calls. A raw SQL transaction is now being drafted to count existing issue labels.

The drafted raw SQL transaction counts existing source-label assignments. It then inserts the target label into matching issues, skipping duplicates via a NOT EXISTS subquery.

The Drizzle query builder is preferred over raw SQL for style consistency. The `mergeLabelAssignments` function is being drafted with an early return when source and target labels are identical.

The function throws an error when merging a label into itself. It fetches all issue IDs assigned to the source label within the organization. Then it queries for existing target-label assignments on those same issues.

The function filters out issues that already carry the target label. It inserts only the remaining missing assignments in a single synchronous run.

The transaction now deletes the source label's issue assignments and the source label row itself. It returns the number of affected issues. A zero-row deletion is possible but unlikely because the service checks label existence first.
